intro: Taiwanese (台語, also called 台灣閩南語) is spoken by most families in Taiwan, especially in the south and among older people. You'll hear it in markets, temples, taxis and on TV, and many Mandarin slang words come from it.

It's written with Chinese characters, often different ones from Mandarin (食 for 吃, 毋 for 不), and with Tâi-lô (台羅), the romanization the Ministry of Education made official in 2006. Older books, churches and signs may use Pe̍h-ōe-jī (POJ) instead, which writes ts as ch and oo as o͘.
In Tâi-lô, hyphens join the syllables of one word (pháinn-sè). A double hyphen marks a light, unstressed syllable after it (tsia̍h-pá--buē).
Phones don't come with Taiwanese voices, so this guide has no sound. The examples use common words you can listen for.

sections.title: 聲母 Consonants
sections.text: Like Mandarin, Taiwanese tells apart unaspirated (p, t, k, ts) and aspirated (ph, th, kh, tsh) consonants. Unlike Mandarin, it also has voiced b, g and j.
rows: like Mandarin b: no puff of air
like Mandarin p: with a puff of air
a real b, as in English "bee"
a real g, as in English "go"
the ng of "sing", at the start
like Mandarin z; before i, like j
like Mandarin c; before i, like q
as in English; before i, like x
like dz; many people say it like l

sections.title: 韻母 Vowels and endings
sections.text: Two things Mandarin doesn't have: nasal vowels (written nn) and short syllables cut off by p, t, k or h.
rows: the vowel goes through the nose; no n sound
back of the tongue stops: short
a catch in the throat: very short

sections.title: 聲調 The tones
sections.text: Tâi-lô numbers the tones 1 to 8. Tone 6 has merged with tone 7 in Taiwan, so there are seven in practice. Tones 4 and 8 are the short ones, ending in p, t, k or h. A favourite way to remember them: 獅、虎、豹、鱉、猴、象、鹿.

sections.title: 變調 Tones change in a phrase
sections.text: In a word or phrase, every syllable except the last changes its tone; only the last keeps the tone you see written. Tâi-lô always writes the original tone, so you change it as you speak. The main circle is 5 → 7 → 3 → 2 → 1 → 7 (in the north, 5 often becomes 3). The short tones swap: 4 → 8 and 8 → 3 (4 ending in h → 2).
rows: 好 hó is said high and level
台 tâi is said middle and level
菜 tshài is said high and falling
